---
title: "Coming from r5r"
description: >
  What is the same as in r5r 2.5.0, and every difference: what peabiru
  does without Java, where its results do not depend on the machine, the
  warnings and errors it adds, and the few inputs it refuses.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("setup.R")
```

peabiru is a drop-in for r5r 2.5.0: it exports the same 22 functions, and a
script written for r5r runs unchanged once the package is swapped. This
page lists what is the same and every difference, on purpose, between the
two. The same list, in the terms of each language, is on the Python and
JavaScript sites. Besides r5r's functions, peabiru has one of its own,
[trip_options()](trip-options.html), which r5r has no counterpart for; it
is not a difference and is not listed here.

## The same

- **Function names, arguments, their order and defaults.** The 22 functions
  r5r 2.5.0 exports have r5r's formals, down to the defaults as expressions
  (`r5r_core = deprecated()`); the one addition is `n_threads` in
  `build_network()`. A test of the package compares them with a snapshot of
  r5r's, so they cannot drift.
- **Argument checks** follow r5r's, in the same order, with the same bounds
  and conversions (a factor `mode`, a POSIXlt `arrival_datetime`) and the
  same messages, word for word (r5r's come from 'checkmate' and 'cli';
  peabiru has ported them without the dependencies).
  `bench/compare/error_parity.R` in the repository calls every function
  with invalid values of every argument in both packages and compares the
  errors.
- **Results**: the same rows, in the same order, with the same column
  names, types and values. For a frequency-based feed this needs the same
  `seed` (without one, both packages draw from the clock and every run
  differs).

Here both packages compute the same matrix on the sample network, and the
results are compared with `identical()`:

```{r, include = FALSE}
# r5r needs a JDK 21; site/build.sh points JAVA_HOME to one when it can.
run_r5r <- requireNamespace("r5r", quietly = TRUE) &&
  nzchar(Sys.getenv("JAVA_HOME"))
```

```{r, eval = run_r5r, message = FALSE}
options(java.parameters = "-Xmx2G")

# r5r writes its network.dat into the data directory: give it a copy
r5r_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "spo")
dir.create(r5r_dir)
invisible(file.copy(list.files(data_path, pattern = "\\.(pbf|zip)$", full.names = TRUE),
                    r5r_dir))
r5r_network <- r5r::build_network(r5r_dir, verbose = FALSE)

args <- list(origins = points, destinations = points,
             mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"), departure_datetime = departure,
             percentiles = c(25, 50, 75), seed = 42, n_threads = 2,
             progress = FALSE)
from_r5r <- do.call(r5r::travel_time_matrix, c(list(r5r_network), args))
from_peabiru <- do.call(peabiru::travel_time_matrix, c(list(network), args))

identical(as.data.frame(from_r5r), from_peabiru)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !run_r5r}
cat("*(This chunk was not run when the page was built: it needs r5r and a JDK 21.)*\n")
```

## How parity is checked {#parity}

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Parity: the same inputs go through r5r 2.5.0 (R5 7.6 on Java) and peabiru, and the outputs are compared for exact equality: matrices pair by pair, accessibility bit for bit, expanded and arrival matrices column by column and in order, and data frames with identical() in R."}
fig("parity.svg")
```

The `identical()` comparison above is how parity is tested: the package's
tests and the scripts in `bench/compare/` in the repository run hundreds of
such comparisons on r5r's Porto Alegre and São Paulo samples (matrices,
accessibility, expanded and arrival matrices, isochrones, itineraries,
fares, elevation, scenarios, network exports, edge cases) and fail on any
difference.

"The same results" is meant literally: every travel time, every
accessibility value (as a double, to the last bit), every row of the
expanded and arrival matrices and of the itineraries, every vertex of the
isochrones, in the same order. This works because the engine is a port of
R5 7.6, the engine r5r drives, and follows its rules down to details that
only matter on ties: the order in which ways, feeds and stops are read,
which of two equal paths is kept, how lengths and speeds are rounded, the
random number generator behind the Monte Carlo draws (a Mersenne Twister
seeded from `seed` and the origin's coordinates, as in R5), and the
exponential of the decay functions (Apache Commons Math's `FastMath.exp`,
which R5 calls, instead of the C library's). Limits are R5's too, such as
the 5,000 destinations accepted by the expanded and arrival matrices.

Two things depend on the platform, in r5r as in peabiru, which follows the
platform it runs on:

<!-- diff:platform-order -->
- **The order of the GTFS feeds.** R5 loads the feeds in the order in which
  the operating system lists the directory, and that order depends on the
  file system. On r5r's Porto Alegre sample (two feeds), r5r on macOS and
  r5r on Linux give the same travel-time matrices and accessibility, but
  227 of the 605,460 rows of the expanded matrix differ (another stop or
  route, a total time up to 0.2 minutes apart). peabiru matches r5r row for
  row on each platform.
- **The rings of isochrone polygons.** 'isoband', which r5r calls, walks a
  C++ hash table whose order decides where each ring starts and in which
  order the rings come; that order depends on the C++ library 'isoband'
  was built with (libc++ on macOS, libstdc++ on Linux and Windows).
  peabiru reproduces both.

## Differences

Everything below is deliberate. Nothing that r5r accepts is silently
ignored or computed differently: where peabiru cannot give r5r's result,
it stops with an error that says so.

### General

<!-- diff:no-java -->
- **No Java.** There is no JVM to start, no `java.parameters` to set and no
  R5 jar to download. r5r's functions for Java are kept so that scripts
  run: `setup_r5()` warns (r5r's deprecation warning) and calls
  `build_network()`; `stop_r5()` removes the given networks (or every
  network in the calling environment) and runs R's garbage collector, with
  r5r's messages; `download_r5()` downloads nothing and returns `NULL`
  invisibly (r5r returns the path of the jar); `r5r_cache()` lists and
  deletes nothing; `r5r_sitrep()` returns `peabiru_package_version`,
  `core_version`, `r5_version`, `r5r_version`, `r_version` and `platform`
  (r5r's has `r5r_package_version`, `r5_jar_version`, `java_version`,
  `set_memory` and `session_info`).

<!-- diff:result-type -->
- **Results are `data.frame`s**, not `data.table`s (also the tables inside
  a fare structure, and the `edges` and `routes` of
  `street_network_to_sf()` and `transit_network_to_sf()`), so the package
  imports nothing. `data.table::setDT()` converts them if you prefer. The
  columns, their order and types and the values are r5r's.

<!-- diff:network-in-memory -->
- **The network lives in memory only.** Nothing is written to the data
  directory (no `network.dat`, no `gtfs_errors.csv`), and the network
  object cannot be saved with `saveRDS()`: build it again in a new
  session, which is quick. `overwrite` and `temp_dir` are checked as r5r
  checks them and have no effect. A network built by `r5r::build_network()`
  is not accepted: build it with `peabiru::build_network()`.

<!-- diff:n-threads-build -->
- **`build_network()` has `n_threads`**, the threads used to read the
  `.pbf` file.

<!-- diff:verbose-progress -->
- **`verbose` and `progress` are checked but print no progress counter**;
  `verbose = TRUE` in `build_network()` reports the build in messages.

<!-- diff:error-classes -->
- **Errors**: where the network's class is named, it is `peabiru_network`;
  r5r's errors from 'cli' are 'rlang' conditions, and peabiru's are plain
  errors with the same text.

<!-- diff:deprecated-args -->
- **Deprecated arguments** (`r5r_core` everywhere, `sample_size` in
  `isochrone()`) are accepted with r5r's warnings, as in r5r.

### Where peabiru's result does not depend on the run or the machine

<!-- diff:gtfs-errors-order -->
- **`get_gtfs_errors()` reads the feeds again** (r5r reads the
  `gtfs_errors.csv` its `build_network()` wrote) and lists the rows feed by
  feed in the order gtfs-lib finds them; r5r's order is that of a Java
  `HashSet` and changes from run to run. The rows and columns are the same.

<!-- diff:elevation-strictmath -->
- **Elevation in projected rasters.** In an elevation raster that is not in
  EPSG:4326, r5r reads one pixel or the other for a street point within
  nanometres (5e-8 m, or 2e-13 degrees) of a pixel boundary or of the
  raster's edge, depending on the last bits of the JVM's sines and cosines;
  peabiru reads the one Java's `StrictMath` gives, on every machine, and
  warns once with the number of such points.

<!-- diff:street-expanded -->
- **Expanded and arrival matrices with a street mode alone.** r5r accepts
  them, but then reports the same trip for every minute of a departure
  time taken from the computer's clock (`Sys.time()`), not from
  `departure_datetime`. peabiru stops with an error; use
  `travel_time_matrix()` for street modes.

Without a `seed`, frequency-based feeds give different results on every run
in both packages; with the same `seed` they give the same.

### Warnings peabiru adds

<!-- diff:elevation-wrapped -->
- **Voids and out-of-range elevations.** R5 keeps elevations in decimetres
  in 16-bit integers, so values beyond +/-3276.7 m wrap around: SRTM's
  -32768 voids become 0 m, a no-data value of -9999 becomes 3108.2 m, a
  `NaN` no-data value 0 m. peabiru stores them as r5r does, so the slope
  costs are r5r's, and warns, counting them and the samples equal to the
  raster's no-data value; r5r is silent.

(The elevation warning above, about points on a pixel boundary, is
peabiru's too.)

### Errors where r5r fails later or routes on wrong values

<!-- diff:errors-instead-of-failures -->
- **Values r5r lets through and then fails on.** peabiru stops with an
  error of its own that says what is wrong for: an empty `percentiles`
  (r5r fails in Java, or in R for isochrones); a missing destination id
  (a `NullPointerException` in Java); an `arrival_datetime` that is not a
  date-time (an internal R error); in `isochrone()`, a `polygon_output` of
  `NA` (r5r takes it as `FALSE` and fails), `origins` without rows (an
  internal R error) and a fractional `zoom` (which r5r passes to R5); in
  `find_snap()`, a `radius` of `NA` or of length 0 (r5r fails in Java); a
  `carspeed_scale` of `NA`, `NaN` or of a length other than 1 (an internal
  R error); in `write_fare_structure()`, something that is not a fare
  structure, settings of the wrong length (r5r checks nothing there and
  fails in `data.table::fwrite()`, or writes tables recycled to the wrong
  length) and a `NULL` `file_path` (r5r fails in `zip::zip()`); in
  `read_fare_structure()`, several files (r5r fails in `zip::unzip()`); a
  fare structure whose fare type is missing from `fares_per_type`, or that
  leaves out a route of the network (r5r fails in Java); in
  `get_gtfs_errors()`, a folder that does not exist.

<!-- diff:scenario-wrap -->
- **Scenarios R5 would corrupt.** R5 keeps car speeds as 16-bit
  centimetres per second. A scenario whose speeds would wrap around or
  reach 0 or less (a negative factor or speed in `new_carspeeds`, a
  polygon `scale` of `Inf` or 0, a `carspeed_scale` far above 1) and a
  `carspeed_scale` beyond the 32-bit float range are errors; r5r routes on
  the wrapped speeds, hands R5 `Infinity`, or fails dividing by zero.
  Polygons that are not valid, and ties between polygons that cannot be
  settled exactly as R5 settles them, are errors too.

### What peabiru refuses

These are the inputs r5r accepts and peabiru does not; each stops with an
error that says so.

<!-- diff:refuse-fare-calculators -->
- **R5's own fare calculators** (a `fare_structure` with a `type`). The
  fare structures of `setup_fare_structure()`, `read_fare_structure()` and
  `write_fare_structure()` are r5r's, and so are the fares computed with
  them.

<!-- diff:refuse-elevation-formats -->
- **Elevation rasters outside what is reproduced exactly**: anything but a
  one-band GeoTIFF, north up, uncompressed or compressed with LZW, Deflate
  or PackBits, in EPSG:4326 or a system whose GeoTools transform peabiru
  reproduces (SIRGAS 2000, SAD69, Córrego Alegre and their UTM zones used
  in Brazil, SIRGAS 2000 / Brazil Polyconic, WGS 84 / UTM, Pseudo-Mercator;
  the list is in `?build_network`), given by its EPSG code; a `.prj` file
  next to the raster; a raster named `.tiff` (r5r fails to read it); more
  than one raster in the directory (r5r reads the last one listed); a
  street point that `StrictMath` puts on a projected raster's outer edge
  (r5r fails there too).

<!-- diff:refuse-multiple-pbf -->
- **More than one `.pbf` file** in the data directory.

<!-- diff:refuse-pareto-output-dir -->
- **`pareto_frontier()` with `output_dir`** (r5r writes the frontier to CSV
  files).

<!-- diff:car-egress-history -->
- **Car egress through turn restrictions with two or more via ways.** In
  `detailed_itineraries()` with `mode_egress = "CAR"`, R5 reverses the via
  edges of such restrictions in place during its egress search, so r5r's
  itineraries for a pair whose car searches cross one can depend on the
  searches that ran before; peabiru returns what r5r gives on a freshly
  built network for that pair alone with one thread, and warns, naming the
  pairs that some other order would change (about 1 pair in 200 on Porto
  Alegre). The arrays are those of the network, which forward car
  searches read too: in r5r, a car matrix, accessibility or Pareto frontier
  computed after such a call could differ as well (none did on Porto
  Alegre: 0 of 344 thousand cells after three calls); peabiru's are those
  of a fresh network.

```{r, error = TRUE}
fares <- setup_fare_structure(network, base_fare = 4.4)
fares$type <- "burlington"
travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
                   departure_datetime = departure, fare_structure = fares)
```

### Files

<!-- diff:write-fare-zip -->
- **`write_fare_structure()`** writes the same CSV files as r5r, deflated
  in the same order, but the archive's bytes differ from r5r's (which also
  holds the files' dates); each package reads the other's files. As in
  r5r 2.5.0, `debug_path` and `debug_info` are kept in the structure and no
  debug file is written.
